utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber has received a motion for trial-related protective measures for Witness 17, who's the next witness in line to testify. We'll briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber has decided that the requested protective measures for Witness 17 are granted, reasons to follow. That means, Mr. Kearney, that we could start the examination of Witness 17 I think for him entering the courtroom the curtains have to be down in relation to face distortion, and then to be opened again once the witness has taken his seat. I also can inform the parties that the suggestions I made during the meeting held this morning on redactions on the 92 ter statement of this witness that my colleagues agree with the guidance I gave. For the public this is just to know that there was some disagreement about what was or was not admissible in the 92 ter statement for this witness to be tendered through him, and that instead of taking a lot of time in court, the Chamber decided to invite the parties for a meeting this morning in order to give the -- to give the parties guidance to resolve this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 17, because that's how we will call you since the Chamber has granted the protective measures requested by the Prosecution just a while ago, protective measures being the use of pseudonym, that means that we'll call you Witness 17 rather than to use your own name; that your face cannot be seen by the outside world; your voice, your own voice, cannot be heard by the outside world, although the content of your testimony is public. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Witness 17, may I invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 17. Please be seated. The curtains can be -- can be raised again. Witness 17, you'll first be examined by Mr. Kearney, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I note that when the witness came into court today he brought with him a satchel of some sort. I don't know if those are documents that are going to be used during the course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 17, whatever you brought I don't know it. You should not consult any documents unless you asked permission to do so. So if you need to consult either any notes or anything else, would you please ask me whether you're allowed to consult these notes rather than to testify just from your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can provide some guidance in that regard. The witness, I believe, has a binder with his original 92 ter statement in it as well as all the annexes that are appended to it. I will ask the Court's permission since we'll be referring to both the statement and the annexes that the witness be allowed to have it in front of him during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you make it clear whenever you invite the witness to consult any of these documents so that's clear because I can't see it from here so we know what is in front of the witness and why and when he uses them. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, good morning. Thank you for coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I would like to call up 65 ter document, if I may 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a pseudonym sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, please look, if you will, at the document on your screen. Look at the information contained on that document, and tell us if that is your personal data and if that is correct, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not receive translation of the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that they cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we should ask the assistance of the technicians. Did you hear the witness when he gave his solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: From the floor, Your Honour, not directly on the earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have to ask the technicians to make sure that the microphone is functioning well. Witness 17, we have to resolve this technical matter first because the interpreters can't hear you. Could you speak one or two words to see whether it's any better now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that it is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that now they can hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- that's fine. Then could you please repeat your answer you apparently gave to the question by Mr. Kearney whether your personal data appeared correctly here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the data that I see on the monitor are correct and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, necessary to draw your attention to the witness information on top of the 92 ter statement gives a different date of birth. I don't know whether you want to clarify that, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, the date of birth that is listed on the sheet on the screen in front of you, is that your correct date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What is your correct date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And we are still in private session, is that correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I would ask that we go into private session for this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there seems to be perhaps similar problem with hearing the witness because I didn't receive translation of his last answer either. But first of all we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we should have waited. So the witness will have copies in front of him, and you will guide him what to consult. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, do you have a binder with your statement and annexes with you today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: You mean do I see them on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: No, do you have a physical binder with you today, including your statement with its annexes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I only see the page of the statement, the last page where I signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 17, we're not talking about what you see on the screen, but whether you have a hard copy of your own statement with the annexes available to you. I can't see it from here, but ... Madam Usher, could you please assist the witness in ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the one that I have in my bag?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney will tell you when and what to look at, but you have got it in front of you. Mr. Kearney, by any chance a hard copy -- I have not seen any of the annexes. Do we only see them on the screen or is there one hard copy for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed they were provided in hard copy to the Court last week -- electronically to the Court last week and it was my understanding that that would be printed out for the members of the Trial Chamber, but perhaps I'm mistaken in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you are. Let's proceed. We'll allow for some additional time for the Chamber to consult what it can find on the screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, I'd like to direct you to paragraph 15, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In this paragraph you detail a meeting you had -- the first meeting you had with Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Balaj on the 26th of June, 1998, in Jasic. I'd like you to describe at the outset, if you can, for the Trial Chambers the relationship between Idriz Balaj, Toger, and Ramush Haradinaj as you observed it during your time in Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, in view of the guidance I gave, I don't think that it would be appropriate for the witness to read now the statement in this respect. If you take him through what you find in paragraph 15, which is of a factual nature, and then ask him to further elaborate on the relationship between Haradinaj and Toger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that guidance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, can you please tell us, just from your memory, the number of times that you saw Idriz Balaj and Ramush Haradinaj together during your time in Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I would say about three to four times that I've seen them together when we had meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The -- the meetings that you saw them together in, can you tell us anything about their travelling to those meetings. Did they come together, did they arrive at the same time, did they come separately, did they leave together? Can you give us more details about that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: This I wouldn't know, but during the meetings that we held with Ramush, especially the first one at Jasic, we were in one room. They came there. Now, as to how they travelled, whether on one car or separately, this I wouldn't be able to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During your time in Kosovo in 1998, did you ever see them travel together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: They were together at the meetings that we had, but I was not there when they travelled together. That's why I wouldn't be able to say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chambers their relationship in terms of military rank, in terms of subordinate/superior, were they equals? Can you tell us anything about that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: As far as ranks are concerned, there weren't any at that time. Nobody was called by his rank, but rather by his position. So when Ramush came to Jasic and had contact with us, he said to us that he was the commander of the Dukagjini Plain, while Idriz Balaj, a.k.a. Togeri, was a commander or his subordinate. He was a commander of the Black Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to clarify your last answer. You said that Togeri was a commander or his subordinate. Whose subordinate was Togeri?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Subordinate of Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Based on your contact with both men and your dealings with the KLA in Kosovo in 1998, can you tell us who it was that Togeri reported to as the head of the Black Eagles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: He wasn't the president but the commander of the Black Eagles. When I said he was Ramush's subordinate, that means that he had to report to Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed Togeri to that position as the commander of the Black Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: This I wouldn't know. I don't know who appointed him and at what time, but when the Dukagjini Plain headquarters was established sometime in the spring of 1998, the staff was formed and the people were appointed to positions within that staff. Maybe Ramush was appointed commander of that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Witness 17. I want to move on now to another area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, may I ask one or two clarifying questions about the relationship between Haradinaj and Balaj during these meetings. Who would be the one who would present the position of that party, who would speak? Was that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the meetings that we had were directly with Ramush, while Idriz Balaj accompanied him, and he was responsible for his security during the travel to and back from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Haradinaj consult with Mr. Balaj during these meetings or was Mr. Balaj just present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he did not consult him. From what I was able to see at those meetings, he did not consult him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, when you say that Idriz Balaj was responsible for Ramush's security during travel to and back from these meetings, can you elaborate on that for us, please. Tell us exactly what his role was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I can only say the following: the Black Eagles were the special unit of the Kosova Liberation Army and was under Ramush's command. At every meeting the travels to Jasic, and later in Prapaqan and in Lluk, the arrival at Baran, the oath that the brigade took, this solemn event, on all these occasions Idriz Balaj was present, too, in the capacity of the person responsible for security because, as I said, the Black Eagles were a special unit. So together --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- As much as I could observe his duty was to provide security for Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, we just spoke of a meeting between the FARK and KLA on the 26th of June, 1998. I want to move now to another contact between the FARK and the KLA which happened on the 4th of July, 1998, this is contained in paragraph 26 of your statement. Now, in that paragraph you describe a conflict between four soldiers of the FARK and Toger and Ramush and other KLA members in Gllogjan on that date. I want to ask you, Witness 17, if this incident affected KLA and FARK relations going forward from that date; and if so, how, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if I might, since this is the first time that there has been a mention of FARK in open testimony, perhaps there should be some clarification of precisely who FARK or what FARK is so that we're proceeding along a better line of understanding what's going on. The word "FARK" was not mentioned or the organisation was not mentioned before Mr. Kearney posed it in a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, we are proceeding on the basis of a 92 ter statement, which of course gives quite some information about the FARK and how it entered Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kearney, page 16, line 16, you introduced a meeting by: "Now we just spoke of a meeting ..." Of course we didn't speak of that meeting at all. Could you please properly introduce that by saying that paragraph so-and-so deals with a meeting or describes a meeting, and then as far as FARK is concerned, first of all, the Chamber of course has received quite some evidence on FARK. It is explained in the earlier paragraphs of the 92 ter statement, so there's no need at this moment to further clarify that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, just by way of background, the first contact that you described earlier between yourself, Mr. Haradinaj, and Mr. Balaj occurred on the 26th of June, 1998, in Jasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Just generally, if you would, we don't want to repeat what's in the 92 ter statement, but if you could just generally outline for us, please, that meeting. What was discussed at that meeting, what was the purpose of it, how long did it last, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I can say that the reason for this meeting was the following: the operative units of the KLA under the command of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Kosova had already entered the Kosovan territory. Since the KLA had already become operative in Kosova and carried out certain activities and because the Dukagjin Plain staff was operative, there started to be frictions between the two from the institutional and organisational point of view. From this point of view, the arrival of Ramush at this meeting was to tell us that there was an organisation present there that should become part of ours. We also had our command, the command of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Kosova, and as professional soldiers it was somehow difficult for us to change our agendas, our plans, our route plans. So we wanted to make it clear to him as well that there was nothing bad in our view that we had arrived there in order to carry out the plans in the phases that we had determined by taking the oath in -- on 21st of June in Tropoje in Albania. So Ramush explained to us the character of the KLA and its activity in the Dukagjini Plain and in the territory where we were, and he said to us that we had to systemize to become part of their command. So as I said, we had already our command and it wasn't that easy to leave to abandon them and to enter another command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And during that first meeting, Witness 17, was an agreement reached between your command and the command of Ramush?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: We were not able to reach a full agreement; however, we made it clear that we were in Kosova to carry out military activities and that we would respect the plans and military strategies in phases, that the first, the second, and the third phase should be carried out. So there was no concrete agreement I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if that's enough of a background I'll now move on to my earlier line of questioning, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, Kearney. I have to apologise for making not a -- I was a bit unfair when I said we did not speak of that meeting at all. We did not speak of that meeting of the 26th of June as a meeting between KLA and FARK. It was just a meeting between persons rather than between two organisations. So I was not very fair as I said it. Please proceed -- perhaps one additional question. You told us that what, as you said, Ramush explained about the character of the KLA and its activity. What -- did you observe anything that would explain why you couldn't reach an agreement? Were your goals different? What was it that kept you off from reaching an agreement on how to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The aim was the same. We both aimed at the liberation of Kosova. We had no disagreements or differences on that. In my opinion, we were told that we were late in joining the war. The war had already started in Kosova, and if we put as a date the attack on Prekaze, that could be the beginning of the war. So some time has passed since, and we were told that we were late in joining the war and that there was an army already in place and that we do not accept other commands from abroad who decide to send units and organise operations in Kosova from abroad, although operations in Kosova should be handled from inside and we -- that we should join the organisation that existed in Kosovo already. These were the differences, but we had our own command and we could not give up the orders of our own command and start implementing orders from another, whereas the KLA wanted to have us under its control and this was why we could not reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, therefore it was a kind of a competition between who would be in command of armed forces and that it was -- yes, I see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we could say that. We could say that it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did Ramush or anyone in -- within the KLA tell you why they wanted you - "you" being the FARK - under their control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that. If you want me to repeat the same. We were told that we were late in joining the war and that the war had already started. We have an organisation already. There is an operative staff in the Dukagjin Zone, and all the rest should join this command and be under the command of this headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness 17, we had begun to talk earlier about a conflict that arose between FARK soldiers and KLA soldiers on the 4th of July, 1998, in Gllogjan. This is described in paragraph 26 in your statement in great detail. I want to ask you if this conflict on that date affected FARK and KLA relations going forward from that date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, surely, because incidents like the one on the 4th of July reflected negatively on the relations amongst ourselves, but we tried to smooth the relations and go forward from there. But again, we have -- we told them openly that incidents like these are intolerable, unacceptable, and they should not happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did that incident impact in any way the FARK's ability to travel within the Dukagjin Zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: It had a negative impact in the sense of affecting the morale of the soldiers because they were informed about what happened on the 4th of July, what happened to the four soldiers of FARK. All soldiers wanted to go in Kosovo and join the war and confront the enemy rather than have problems amongst ourselves. In a way, it had a negative impact; on the other hand, a kind of uncertainty was created among the soldiers. If we were to send them somewhere to carry out an operation, they didn't know what was going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that, please. Explain what you mean by an uncertainty being created among the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: A kind of insecurity I said because of what happened, because of this incident. They were skeptical in as -- in carrying out their duties, their future duties. So there was this insecurity, this fear, that if they were to be sent somewhere to carry out a task they would face obstacles, and they wouldn't be in a position to carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Obstacles presented by whom, Witness 17?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: We are talking about the incidents -- the incident between the soldiers of the FARK and the military people of the headquarters in Gllogjan, because this incident took place in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to talk to you, if I may, about another conflict between FARK soldiers and the KLA which occurred on the 10th of July of 1998 in Prapaqan. You detail this event in paragraph 41 of your statement. In the third full sense of that statement you say, quoting: "I noticed a group of approximately 15 KLA soldiers dressed in black standing in the yard pointing their rifles towards the barracks entrance in a state of combat-readiness." I would like to ask you: Which unit were those soldiers wearing black?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: It was the special unit of the KLA, the Black Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: On that day in Prapaqan, this is 10 July of 1998, who was leading them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: They came together with Togeri and Ramush, and as I said earlier their leader was Togeri.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, I would like to direct you, if I may, to the second-to-the-last sentence of that paragraph in which you state that: "He," being Ramush, "accused us of being Milosevic collaborators and said, 'You officers have 30 minutes to leave the premises or it will become a fratricide.'" ? I want to ask you if you ever heard Ramush on another day use that word "collaborator"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: On another day or the same day are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: On a different date. On any of the approximately 20 times you had contacts with Mr. Haradinaj during the time you were in Kosovo, did he ever express a concern to you about collaborators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: No, no. On this occasion, on the 10th of July when they came to the barracks of Prapaqan, that's when this term was used. At that moment Ramush was not himself. There was no self-control. He was frustrated and I couldn't tell what the reasons were for that, and he said what he said. In other words, we were given an ultimatum to leave the barracks within 30 minutes, and the pretext for this was a row between him and Tahir Zemaj in the kitchen because our soldiers, that is, FARK soldiers, they greeted, they saluted, a stretched hand, whereas the KLA soldiers who were -- had already been organised in form of an army before we arrived, they saluted with a fist. And because of this difference as far as saluting was concerned, the confrontation broke out and the incident happened between Ramush and Tahir, and it continued in the barracks, as described in the statement on paragraph 41 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And also in that paragraph, Witness 17, you use the word "fratricide" as being threatened by Ramush during that -- during -- on that date. Was that the actual word he used when he was speaking with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: This incident could very well lead to a war -- to a war between brothers, as it were, and could lead to a bloodbath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to carefully listen to the question put to you by Mr. Kearney. Mr. Kearney was not asking what could have been the consequences but whether the word "fratricide" was used literally at that moment by Mr. Haradinaj. That was the question. Would you please answer the question. You're invited to -- your statement is clear in that respect. Mr. Kearney is checking your memory, whether that in your recollection was the actual word he used at that moment. If you don't know, please tell us; if you do know ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me whether this word was uttered by Ramush, it's difficult to say now nine years on. But the very fact that he fired above our heads with his Kalashnikov and the ultimatum that we were given showed that it was close to fratricide. But I cannot say specifically whether he uttered that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, I want to move on to a different topic, if I may, this is -- the discussion we're going to have relates to paragraph 45 of your statement, specifically to the latter portion of that paragraph, I believe it's the second-to-the-last sentence. I'm going to quote this for you and ask you to comment on it. "Tahir Zemaj got letters every day from villagers complaining about KLA behaviour, both in our AOR," A-O-R, I assume that means area of responsibility, "as well as in KLA AORs. I saw and read the letters." I want to ask you, Witness 17, can you tell us, please, anything in more detail about those letters. What were the -- for instance, what were the complaints being made by villagers regarding the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: The letters were describing incidents that had taken place and -- like the ones that we described earlier, because the local population was familiar with such incidents and that was causing a loss of confidence among the population and in their letters they asked from the -- from the commanders -- they were asking that the command of the Dukagjin area be under Tahir Zemaj and this was a demand by the territorial headquarters from the villages in the area where Tahir and his operative units, Operational Staff units were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say, Witness 17, that these letters --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might just for the purposes of the proceedings there will be a standing objection here for lack of foundation, unsourced information, no ability to adequately, at any point, meet this information at a later point in time unless Mr. Kearney can produce sources and/or documents that establish what the witness is claiming at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kearney is invited to get as much details in this respect as possible. The objection as such is denied to the extent that we will not prohibit Mr. Kearney from further questioning the witness about it and it will not result in a non-admission of the lines just quoted by Mr. Kearney. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, you say that these letters described incidents that had taken place like the ones that we described earlier. Can you tell us what those are, please. What types of incidents were these letters complaining about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: What I was saying is that in their letters they were demanding that the command of the Dukagjini Zone be under Tahir Zemaj and that professional officers, military officers, be in command. And secondly, the incidents that we mentioned earlier, which was our going into Jasic and blocking the armed forces there and us not being allowed to pass through Junik and then the other incident was the beating of the four soldiers on the 4th of July, and then the other incident on the 10th of July. And all these irritated the local population, and all this irritation and frustration led to the writing of these letters. We cannot have a document for every single word, but there is a document which I have already handed over. I gave it to Hashim Thaqi, and that one showed that the incidents like these had taken place and that had caused a lot of frustration among the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness might remove his earphones at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether the witness understands any English. Witness 17, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understand, but not well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm in Your Honours' hands as to how to proceed in that respect. The basis for the objection to this part of the evidence was discussed in a meeting this morning. It's now been explored by Mr. Kearney and the answers that the witness has given do not support the basis for which the Prosecution sought to adduce this material. Now, I'm prepared to leave the matter there at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would seek clarification, as a matter of fact, rather than anything else. And I might take an initiative in this moment. Witness 17, you -- in your statement you say that villagers were complaining about KLA behaviour. Asked about the incidents they referred to in their letters, as far as I understand, you mainly referred to incidents in which, at least at first eye, it wasn't the villagers but it was rather FARK soldiers that were bothered through these incidents. Is that what the villagers were writing about, about the inconvenience of these incidents by -- the inconvenience experienced by FARK soldiers or was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said earlier, I probably repeat it again, such letters arrived from the regional headquarters of the Territorial Defence in the villages, because every village had its own Territorial Defence headquarters. And such concerns existed I said on the part of the villagers, but they were connected to the headquarters. They were -- they were acquainted with the incidents through these regional headquarters, and that's how they came to write these letters, through which they asked for Tahir Zemaj to be leading, to be the chief commander of the Operational Staff zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were letters not of ordinary villagers but of their -- but of their local people in charge asking for a change -- asking for Tahir Zemaj to be the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember how many of these letters you have seen approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At a meeting in Broliq, the last meeting we had, I personally took those letters from Tahir Zemaj and I gave it -- them to Fadil Haderxhonaj who was responsible in Tahir Zemaj's brigade and I asked him to take those letters to the people in charge at the KLA General Staff and they were taken to Hashim Thaqi. He saw these letters. He only kept one letter, the rest he threw away. He tore them to bits and threw them away on the floor, he threw them on the floor in the room. I cannot remember how many exactly they were, but I could say there were tens of those letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, you mentioned two terms that I want to inquire with you about in greater detail. One was "Territorial Defence" and one was "local villagers." Can you tell us in your mind if those are the same thing, are they different. Can you explain the relationship between those two groups, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: There weren't separate groups. The villagers were ordinary people who were involved in the organisation of the units in their own villages. The Territorial Defence, on the other hand, were some elderly people and you could have people ranging from 35 to 60 years old, and they were all involved in the defence of their own village. Others were younger people from 18 years upwards, who were either members of the KLA or FARK units. So when we talk about local villagers and the Territorial Defence we could give this sort of explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In any of these --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: The difference being just in terms of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In any of these tens of letters that you were referring to, was there ever any mention or complaint of criminal activity being undertaken by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: No, I haven't come across such letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In those circumstances, given the basis upon which this material was put forward, we again renew our objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, I'd now like to move on to -- or to discuss a meeting that you had with Mr. Haradinaj on either the 10th or the 11th of July, 1998, which is detailed in paragraph 50 of your statement. In the second sentence of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I object -- I object to the form of this examination, both in relation to the way in which it's presented by reference to the 92 ter statement and in the way in which Mr. Kearney seeks to go to the second sentence. Paragraph 50 needs to be read in conjunction with paragraph 40 for any proper examination of this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. One second. Yes, perhaps, Mr. Kearney, if you want to elicit evidence in relation to paragraph 50 perhaps do not take the witness to the -- to his statement but rather elicit that evidence in -- not using the statement, although you may refer to that a meeting was held on the 10th of July and then ask the witness whether he remembers what he raised during that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it had been my intent to, in discussing paragraph 50, ask this witness why he asked Mr. Haradinaj to dismiss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ask him -- okay. But do it without -- I mean, if we are seeking clarification or if we are seeking further -- further information about these events, then please do not use the text of the statement given because it might be that apart from it being an introduction that, the witness also reads portions of which we try to elicit his evidence without specific reference to his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, on 10 or 11 July 1998, I believe in the village of Luka, did you request of Ramush Haradinaj that he either dismiss or discipline Toger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, in a way I did draw his attention to this issue because the previous day there was an instant at the traffic junction between Prilep and Gllogjan, and this was an incident between myself and Idriz Balaj. I was going to the military hospital to visit a friend who was wounded during the first attack -- operation in Loxha, and Togeri asked me for a permit, whether I was allowed to move around. Initially I tried to consider it as a joke, but when he insisted then I reacted, and I asked him whether he knew me, who I was. He said, No, I don't know you, and then I told him if he remembered the meeting at Jasic and -- and then someone -- then I tried to give him some detail and said it was me there in that room. Then I -- I showed him an automatic weapon and a few hand-grenades, and then that was what caused the incident and I told him that I was the commander of a brigade, and I had permission to move around the area and that nobody could stop me from going to the military hospital to visit a friend. And that is why I asked Ramush to either dismiss him or to discipline him, because incidents like these could lead to greater consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say -- first of all, before we explore that last statement, were you in uniform when this contact with Toger took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, I was wearing a uniform at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What type of permit was Idriz Balaj demanding of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I really don't know. He just asked for a permit, for an authorisation that would allow me to be there in that territory. I don't know in concrete terms what he had in mind, because we didn't have a lengthy conversation. He asked for permission, and I told him that for me an authorisation to be there were the automatic rifle and the hand-grenades that I took from the battle in Loxha. And I made it clear to him that I had to go there to the military hospital and pay a visit to my senior officer who was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say that contacts such as the one you had with Idriz Balaj could lead to greater consequences, what did you mean by that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Well, such incidents created frustrations amongst ourselves, and you know that when one is frustrated he cannot carry out his activities properly, he cannot fulfil tasks properly in the designated area. And this can only grow and grow and lead to something bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, when we left off, we were talking about a meeting you had with Mr. Haradinaj on 10 or 11 July 1998 in Luka, and tell us on that day did you ask Mr. Haradinaj to discipline Togeri based on what had happened after the first battle at Loxha?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the witness does not receive translation. Still -- of course we have to speak a few words in order to test the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation. I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear you, yes, and you can repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When we left off we were talking about a meeting you had with Mr. Haradinaj on 10 or 11 July 1998 in Luka, when you asked Mr. Haradinaj to discipline or dismiss Togeri. Can you please tell us what Mr. Haradinaj said during that meeting to you when you asked him that question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we first establish on what basis this witness was asking for dismissal or disciplinary action; in other words, what the nature of the complaint was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily to be done by Mr. Kearney. If you would like to -- of course it raises a question, but I leave it to Mr. Kearney whether he wants to raise it or whether he should do it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: If it will make it clear, Your Honour, I would be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, please tell us why it was you were asking to have Togeri disciplined or dismissed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I assumed that his behaviour during the Isniq incident was not a proper behaviour and that's why I asked Ramush to do something about it, to discipline Togeri, because when that occurred we were no strangers to each other. We had already met each other on several occasions. We knew each other very well, and he knew very well what was my role and position in that zone. And that's why I found it illogical, I mean his behaviour illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What had Togeri done wrong in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: It was a provocation on his part addressed at a person, that is, me, who was there with a certain task. He knew very well that I was operative, that I operated with my units there, that I was a commander of a brigade, and that's why I took it as a provocation, his questions as to why I was there and him asking me to produce an authorisation when I already explained to him that I was on my way to visit a wounded colleague, a colleague that was wounded during the Loxha battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And what did Ramush say when you asked him -- you told him about Togeri's actions and asked him to take some disciplinary action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: He smiled. He said to me, Yes, I know, Toger told me about this, but it wasn't a good thing from your side to do, to show him your weapon. But I will speak to him. This is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Based on your own observations, after that meeting of Toger and Ramush, was Toger ever disciplined for the interaction you had with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was initially going to object because it called for speculation. He said based on his observations. Now he says he has no knowledge of this. So it's a question of, once again, of whether or not he's speculating as to whether or not there was any discipline or if there need be any discipline, if there was any basis for discipline. There are a whole series of predicates that are being assumed here that are not necessarily relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney just wanted to know from this witness whether he was aware of any disciplinary action taken against Toger at the time. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After that discussion that you had with Mr. Haradinaj in early July of 1998, from your own observations did Togeri retain his role as the commander of the Black Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Mr. Haradinaj on another occasion or any other occasions to discipline Togeri?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Later there was a meeting between Tahir and Ramush when the Operational Staff command in the Dukagjini Plain was formed, and this is when we discussed these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that conversation with Mr. Haradinaj was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: As I said, it was when the command of the Dukagjini Plain was established, around the 21st of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Regarding that date, the 21st of June, Witness 17, is that correct? I understand from your statement you didn't arrive in Kosovo until after that date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, I want to clarify here. I meant 21st of August, because we are speaking about the month of July at the moment. What I meant was 21st of August. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: On that occasion when you asked Mr. Haradinaj to discipline Togeri, why were you asking on that occasion? What had he done wrong in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: It was said that his behaviour were not suitable to the time and the activities, and through those letters that we received before, we had knowledge that something was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And what was the knowledge of things you had that were wrong that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: As I said, these incidents and his contact from the very beginning to that particular time. It was said that Toger's behaviour was of special kind compared to the behaviour of other fighters and commanders. The population was also irritated by his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What was the special kind of behaviour you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I mentioned the incidents that had occurred up to that moment and the letters that we received from the staffs of Tahir Zemaj. And Tahir also had personal conversations with other persons, from which he learned that Toger's behaviour was not proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: On this second occasion that you asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I interpose the standing objection that I have with regard to this kind of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness 17, could you be more specific. You say: "Tahir also had personal conversations with other persons." Were you present during these conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't there when he spoke to these persons, but pursuant to the military hierarchy and command we did speak with each other on these matters. If I was in another place, than him, it doesn't mean that our contacts were not daily. We did have daily contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that in your conversations he told you about those conversations with other persons. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he tell you what kind of persons these were? Were these ordinary citizens or were they persons in any specific position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were ordinary villagers who had experienced different types of things, let's say whose family members were maltreated or beaten or who didn't know about their family members, about their whereabouts. These were persons from these villages who had their family members gone missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how in these conversations, how could these ordinary villagers establish a link between Toger and their missing family members, because that's what you said, these were complaints about behaviour of Toger. How did they explain that Toger was involved? Did they explain that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tahir had said that if someone was detained and sent -- taken to Gllogjan and if his whereabouts are unknown, then it is Toger's responsibility who carried out these detentions. And that's why the villagers were interested in these things and provided Tahir with information on these incidents, since something was wrong. It was said that the missing persons, those that were detained and who went missing, these persons were sent to Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you said Tahir had said that if someone was detained that it's Toger's responsibility. Did he explain why he blamed Toger for that or not someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he reached these conclusions and he collected this information through these conversations with these persons. I don't know in details what he spoke with persons who visited him in the military premises, but he did have such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm left with a lack of clarity so far as my client is concerned in response to questions and answers that have just preceded that interchange whether this witness is contending that specific allegations of particular offences were reported to Mr. Haradinaj at this meeting as having been committed by Idriz Balaj; in other words, whether the witness is in a position to relate any specific allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although this could have been asked in cross-examination, I take it, Mr. Kearney, that there's no objection against -- when this matter was raised during this meeting, the - as it was said - the behaviour of Toger which was not proper, were any specific incidents raised during that meeting or was it just a general complaint about what Toger was supposed to be responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no specific incidents were mentioned. We spoke about this in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It seems, based on the responses received, once again we're talking about that fatal and dangerous beast known as rumour. I don't know what, if any, weight or the extent of weight that the Chamber would give to this but I would point out that I'm left in a position where I virtually cannot do any kind of cross-examination with regard to these kinds of allegations based upon the state of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's perfectly clear. Mr. Guy-Smith, I take it that it must be clear to you by now that the Chamber, in addition to the parties, endeavours to clearly find out what the basis for whatever allegations there are, and I would say the weaker the sources are the less probative value of course the material gains. But at the same time, as I've said at various occasions including during the meeting this morning, that the final assessment, the final evaluation of the evidence will be done on the basis of the whole, but for every single detail of the evidence the Chamber tries to get as good an impression as possible as to how solid or insolid the material is on which we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Consider. Mr. Kearney, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, I want to direct you to paragraph 109 of your statement where you talk about this meeting that you and Mr. Zemaj had with Mr. Haradinaj. In the second sentence of that paragraph you state that you told Mr. Haradinaj that KLA members, Maliq Ndrecaj, Faton Mehmetaj, and Idriz Balaj should be removed from his Dukagjini staff as these members were committing crimes against civilians. I want to ask you, is that true, did you tell Mr. Haradinaj that these men were committing crimes against civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: When the staff or the Joint Command of the Dukagjini Plain was established on the basis of this agreement on the 21st of August, a joint meeting was held, but this command did not comprise of these persons except for Faton Mehmeti, who remained there. That's why myself and Tahir made it very clear that those persons who were involved in such incidents should not be part of the command. We have later on the case of Sanije Balaj, we had information that she was missing, and we collected information about how it happened from her detention to the moment she was dead. So based on information of this nature, we asked for such persons not to be part of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when you asked Mr. Haradinaj during this meeting to remove those men from his command, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: He said that he was aware about the rumours concerning Toger and his doings. He said that he would speak to others, but I don't know if he did. However, we continued to witness a same situation, persons remaining in the positions that they held in the past. We didn't see any change in the structure, in the military structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to now follow-up on activities of the KLA directed at civilians, specifically to a list of wanted persons that you describe in paragraph 57 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And I would like to call up annex number 1 which is 65 ter number 757 in this regard. And with the Court's permission I'm going to ask that we show page 13 of the English translation on the screen. I believe the witness has his own copy of his original notes in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are shown to him on the screen, it should not be for the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. If we could scroll down a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, when Mr. Kearney says that the witness has his original notes with him, I understand that to mean that these are notes that very authored by him and are in his handwriting or created at his direction. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I should state, the document he's looking at in Albanian is in Xeroxed copy of his handwritten notes that he made back in the -- in 1998 at the time in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, I'd like to ask you when you received or how you came to make this entry into your notes, this list of wanted persons. Please tell us how you came to have that information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I will try to explain. At around 12th of July, the operative unit was established in Baran e Vogel, and we held a meeting at Vranovc with the commander of Lugu i Baranit as it was called at that time, Din Krasniqi, and with certain village commanders whom I didn't know at that time. During this meeting, I was given this list, and I have written in my diary, I have made this entry on the next day, the 13th, when we were inspecting the terrain, trying to find the best option for setting up the military premises. So we went to Baran e Vogel, and we came to a conclusion that the village school would be the most appropriate place. So what I'm trying to say is that I didn't make up this list but this list was given to me during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And do you know who this list was given to you by, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I don't know, but it is possible that this list was made an entry by a person who was taking the minutes, Din Krasniqi or someone else, but I'm not able to tell you who exactly provided that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us if it was someone within the KLA who gave you this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: This was a meeting with a representative of the KLA for the Lugu i Baranit, Din Krasniqi, and the village commanders. So if you look at it this way you can well say that these were the persons who had made this list and who had brought it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: At the time you made these notes or you transcribed this list into your notes, did these names mean anything to you, the names on this list --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And by the way, there's a second page, members of the Trial Chamber, of this wanted list. Perhaps we could show that at this time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, the ten names on this list, did any of them mean anything to you at that time when you were taking them -- when the list had been given to you by a KLA member?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, that's not what the witness testified to. That's a misstatement of the witness's testimony as to who gave -- who gave him the list. He said he did not know who the list came from, that it could be from either village commanders or either from KLA representatives --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I would submit the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would submit it is not the same thing at all and Mr. Kearney knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I would completely object to my colleague's last statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The last statement was -- the objection is fine, Mr. Guy-Smith, but the suggestion that Mr. Kearney is with intent misleading the witness is perhaps not at this point in time appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Shall I rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you rephrase it. I'm just re-reading exactly what the answer was. Yes, I take it that -- Witness 17, perhaps before you rephrase the question. You earlier said it was at a meeting with the representative for the KLA at Lugu i Baranit, Din Krasniqi and the village commanders. Commanders of what type? Were these civilian people in charge or were they KLA commanders for that village or was it -- what exactly did you mean by "village commanders"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were commanders of the villages or representatives of the villages for the KLA. When we arrived there, almost every village had a representative of theirs who was called the commander of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do I understand that now from your answer that "commander" means those in command of the KLA in that village? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, commanders who were responsible for their respective villages. They were the persons in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but now you leave out in your answer one thing I included in my question, that if you say they were the persons in charge, would that necessarily link them to KLA activities or could it be unrelated to KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't speak in any concrete terms. They were responsible or persons in charge for their respective villages in organisational terms. They were in charge of the organisation and the activities in the villages, these commanders. So they participated in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you mean that commanders could be persons who were not having any position in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were called commanders of villages. This is how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some did and some others, due to the shortage of uniforms, didn't have any. Not all the soldiers were uniformed, and I'm speaking about the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this to understand that those who were not in uniform did not have any position different from those who were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who did not have uniforms but were engaged in the activities of the village in standing guard or so on, you can call them members of the Territorial Defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'd like to move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, earlier we were talking about a list of ten. I'd -- I'd like to look again at page 13, where I find eight names. Then I'd like to move on to page 14, where we start with some text and then continue with 9 and 10. Are these names under 9 and 10 also persons wanted or missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are in the same list, I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up annex 14, 65 ter number 724, if I may, this is, I believe, a list of military police regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And again, Witness 17, I'd like to direct you to annex 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And perhaps on our screens we could bring up the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, if you bring up for the witness the English, wouldn't it be better to have the original one for him because we can easily link to the English translation on our computers and it would certainly help the witness to see it in the original language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: However you would like, Your Honour. He has a hard copy in front of him at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, first of all, please tell us how you came to be in receipt of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Upon the establishment of the general command in the Dukagjin Zone on the basis of an agreement between FARK and the KLA, basically between Ramush and Tahir Zemaj, this -- these set of regulations came because Tahir was the deputy and this was in the archives as a document, and Tahir in Prapaqan, where I was the head of the staff in Kryshec, he gave me a copy for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And do you know how this document came into your archives originally, who brought it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I don't know who brought it there, but it's a document of the KLA and it was of the Operational Staff of the plain of Dukagjin and it was signed by Commander Ramush Haradinaj. How it was brought there I cannot say, but I -- as I said, it was soon after the formation of the Joint Command that this document may have been brought by Ramush, because the contacts started to intensify with -- with Ramush. We had more contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the letterhead on the Albanian original when you say "the Operational Staff of the plain of Dukagjin," was that a letterhead that you had seen before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, it says the Kosovo Liberation Army Operational Staff of the plain of Dukagjin. It coincides with the -- all documents which were drafted by the staff of which Ramush Haradinaj was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'd like to scroll down, if I may, to the third item on this list of military police regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Kearney, the witness said it was signed by Ramush Haradinaj. In the original I -- at least the original as I find it in my computer system that needs some clarification. We could scroll down to the -- in the original to the -- yes. You said the document was signed, Witness 17. I find a name under it but no signature. Could you explain your answer that this document was signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it writes "Ramush Haradinaj," but we may have misunderstood each other. I can see that there is no signature there, but it writes, his name is written on there and there is no signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the third item on the list of military police regulations. And it says: "The PU," or military police, "has the task of investigating and uncovering with persuasive facts all those who collaborate in any way with the enemy." First of all, is that an accurate translation? Is that what the original reads in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I can read it in the Albanian language. The regulations were written in the Albanian language, that was the original language. I cannot believe it that it has been translated from another language other than the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, you are quoting in the English language and you're asking the witness whether it's an accurate translation. Now, it's retranslated into his own language, to the witness. How could he possibly answer that question? Or would you like him to look at the English as such, but then we should ask him whether his mastery of the English language is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That's a point well taken, Your Honour. I can move on. I want to ask him about a particular phrase in that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, the item says that: "The military police had the task of uncovering those persons who collaborate in any way with the enemy." I want to ask you if anywhere on that document there is a definition of what "collaboration" or "collaboration in any way" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could -- first of all, before the witness answers the question, if the verbatim statement could be read because it has another series of component parts that have been left out of the question, such as "investigating" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think of course everyone could try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm saying this, Your Honours, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- As presently constituted doesn't deal with an internal -- and in many senses internal definition which has: "Has a task of investigating and uncovering with persuasive facts," so the question of persuasive facts becomes paramount to the determination of how one would define "collaboration" as it's written in the regulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All I'm asking is he ask the question giving the verbatim regulation. That's all I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And I did that originally, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think originally you quoted the whole of the line and then asked whether it was a correct translation. I can imagine that the parties will have further questions on the language of paragraph 3, but at this moment, Mr. Kearney, your question to the witness was - and he can answer that question - what to collaborate in any way with the enemy means -- whether that's -- I think it's whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Defined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Defined. Yes. Again, Mr. Kearney, that question again, we can all read that document. Do you think that there's any doubt as to whether there is or there is no definition of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I can rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did the -- Witness 17, did the Operational Staff of the Plain of Dukagjin, to your knowledge, ever issue a definition of "collaboration"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: The word itself "collaboration" means those who work with the enemy and in every way and on every occasion work against the interests of the people. This is what we mean by a collaborator. If we talk about cooperation, we're talking about those people who are working with the enemy against the interests of the population. This is the word -- what the word "collaboration" means. But as far as this text is concerned, I believe that these are the words which were written initially in the original language, in the Albanian language, and then they were translated into English. And this is how this regulation was drafted originally. Whether -- as to when and who drafted it, I cannot say because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honours. I want to, in the interests of time, direct the witness to paragraphs 100 through 103 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In these paragraphs, Witness 17, you detail a meeting that took place in Prapaqan on 20 August 1998 that was attended by 68 village commanders. Can you please tell the Trial Chambers, what was the purpose of that rather large meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Yes, it was known that at the time, the beginning of August, up until the 13th of August there was a massive offensive in the Lugu of Baran and the villages of Gjakove and the aim was to destroy the Operational Staff units and the KLA where it was operating. For this reason, after the 10th of August, Gllogjan fell to the enemy, Irzniq did the same, and the other villages which appear on this statement. There was a joint demand of that only by joining in a unified command we can confront the enemy and face the enemy successfully. And Ramush came to the conclusion that something must be done to form this Joint Command. He had contacts with Tahir, and this led to the meeting of Prapaqan with participation of 68 representatives from the villages in the area, Ramush was there, together with Tahir and myself. We chaired that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say that the -- Ramush, Tahir, and yourself chaired that meeting, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: I mean that we explained the offensives and how we had come to this point that so many villages had fell -- had fallen to the enemy and what should be done in the future. It was aimed at a re-organisation, restructuring of the forces in that region in order to conduct military operations and confront and face the enemy in battles like those. So we conducted a detailed analysis of what had happened up until then and what should be done in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, also during that meeting did an individual --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And for this, perhaps, Your Honour, we should go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Your Honours. We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 17, this FARK member who got up and addressed the room during this meeting made statements that you recount in paragraph 101. I want to have you -- I'm going to refer to that paragraph for a moment. And in the fourth sentence from the bottom you state, quoting, that: "He asked for the KLA to be disciplined and well-behaved and to stop committing these crimes." I want to ask you if this FARK member told the group that day what crimes he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: Now I cannot go into the details of what he meant and -- but he said that fish was getting fat on human flesh in Lake Radoniq, and I'm referring to the fact that there were several people who'd gone missing and there was detailed information about Sanije Balaj, the case of Sanije Balaj. He did not, in fact, speak specifically, but he spoke on general terms; and he called for these crimes to be stopped. It was difficult to get into his head because he was not specific in what he said. He didn't give out details, but he mentioned the crimes in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When he said that he was calling for these crimes to be stopped, who was he calling on to stop committing these crimes? What -- what people was he directing those comments to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/17
utterances.text: He was calling on persons who were members of the KLA, and he was referring -- he meant these people, and it later came out that all the people who turned out to be missing, all these cases were caused by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This comment that he made, quoting: "The fish in Lake Radoniq were getting fat on human flesh" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interpose an objection to the legal statement made at the end of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, objections are there to stop the other party from putting further -- I mean it's more or less comment on what you're saying is that this is a legal conclusion, which is of course perfectly clear to the Chamber as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
